question.text: Mr. Arjun Kapoor is stress-testing a portfolio that is 70% allocated to a Nifty-50 index ETF (standard deviation 18% p.a.) and 30% to Chambal Managed Futures Fund (a Cat III CTA-style strategy with standard deviation 22% p.a.). Historical correlation between the two is −0.20. Using the two-asset portfolio-variance formula, what is the portfolio standard deviation (approx.)?

answer.text: About 19.2% — close to the weighted average of the two standard deviations
About 13.2% — the negative correlation reduces variance substantially
About 6.6% — correlation alone drives variance to near-zero
About 22.0% — portfolio risk equals the riskier asset

explanation.text: **The Logic:** σp^2 = w1^2·σ1^2 + w2^2·σ2^2 + 2·w1·w2·ρ·σ1·σ2 = 0.7^2·18^2 + 0.3^2·22^2 + 2·0.7·0.3·(−0.20)·18·22 = 0.49·324 + 0.09·484 + 2·0.21·(−0.20)·396 = 158.76 + 43.56 + (−33.26) = 169.06. σp = √169.06 ≈ 13.0–13.2%. The negative correlation of −0.20 delivers a meaningful diversification benefit versus the weighted-average SD of about 19.2%. **The Trap:** Option A is the weighted-average SD — the naive (wrong) computation that ignores correlation. Option C over-states the diversification benefit — correlation of −0.20 does not eliminate variance. Option D ignores the 70/30 split and the diversification effect entirely. **Cross-Exam Context:** XV (Research Analyst) and XXI-B (Portfolio Manager) both test the same two-asset variance formula. X-A/B (Investment Adviser) expects the same computation for financial planning. **Manager's Pro-Tip:** Cat III managed-futures/CTA strategies are prized precisely because their historical correlation to equities is near zero or negative. Before sizing the sleeve, run a rolling 36-month correlation — regimes shift, and 2008-style crises have seen diversification benefits compress when the fund needed them most. Do not mistake long-run historical correlation for a risk-management promise.
